posts.title: 32k tokens per tool call math
posts.hook: Claude's agent SDK defaults to 32k tokens per tool call. Do the math on what that means for a 10-step agentic loop.
posts.body:
Claude's agent SDK defaults to 32k tokens per tool call. Do the math on what that means for a 10-step agentic loop.

320k tokens. One task. One agent run.

I've been running Claude Code as my daily driver for six months. The token bills are real. Last month I burned through ~$400 in API credits on content ops alone... and I'd do it again because the output replaced two tools I was paying $600/mo for.

The trick isn't reducing token usage. It's routing correctly.

🔧 Small deterministic tasks get a script, not an agent
🔧 Research tasks get a subagent with a tight scope
🔧 Multi-file builds get plan mode first, execution second

Most people see the token bill and flinch. But compare it to what you're actually replacing. A Clay seat. A Jasper subscription. Three Zapier automations. A VA.

The real cost isn't tokens. It's letting an agent run unbounded because you didn't define the exit condition.

I cap every subagent with a single deliverable. One task, one output, done. My main context stays clean, and the bill stays predictable.

If your agent loops are expensive, the problem isn't the model. It's the orchestration.

remixes.body:
I spent $400 on AI agent tokens last month. My CFO asked if I'd lost my mind. Then I showed her the spreadsheet.

The $400 replaced two SaaS tools billing $600/mo combined. Net savings: $200/mo. But that's not the real math.

The real math is time. Those two tools required me to context-switch between dashboards, copy-paste outputs, and manually QA results. That was 6-8 hours a week of glue work.

Now a single Claude Code session handles the same pipeline in 20 minutes. I point it at a task, it burns through 320k tokens across a 10-step agentic loop, and I get a finished deliverable.

People fixate on the token cost without measuring what it displaces. $400 sounds expensive until you realize it's buying back 30 hours of skilled labor per month.

The mistake most teams make: they compare agent costs to zero. As if the alternative is free. The alternative is your time, your salary, your opportunity cost of not shipping the next thing.

I track every dollar in a tokens ledger. Total API spend, task category, output quality. Not because I'm cheap. Because I want to know exactly where the leverage is highest.

Six months of data says the leverage is in orchestration tasks. Anything that requires reading five inputs, synthesizing, and producing a structured output. That's where agents print money.
remixes.cta: Are you tracking your agent ROI against the tools and hours they replace? Or just looking at the invoice?

remixes.label: hidden-costs-breakdown
remixes.hook: Everyone talks about the cost of running AI agents. Nobody talks about the cost of running them wrong.
remixes.body:
Everyone talks about the cost of running AI agents. Nobody talks about the cost of running them wrong.

32k tokens per tool call is the default in Claude's agent SDK. Most people never change it. That means a sloppy prompt that triggers 15 tool calls just burned 480k tokens doing something a well-structured 3-call loop could handle in 96k.

The difference between a $50/mo agent habit and a $500/mo one isn't how much you use agents. It's how you structure the calls.

Three things I learned the expensive way:

1. Context window management is the actual skill. Stuffing everything into one massive prompt is the AI equivalent of SELECT *. Scope your inputs.

2. Tool call count is your multiplier. Every unnecessary step compounds. A 10-step loop that should be 4 steps costs 2.5x more with identical results.

3. Caching changes the economics completely. Repeated prompts with static system instructions should hit cache. If they don't, you're lighting money on fire.

I cut my monthly spend by 40% without reducing output. Not by using agents less. By using them with more intention.

The token bill is feedback. It tells you exactly how disciplined your agent architecture is.

posts.title: CRM field massacre
posts.hook: We had 23 fields on our CRM contact object. I deleted 14 of them last week.
posts.body:
We had 23 fields on our CRM contact object. I deleted 14 of them last week.

Nobody noticed for three days. That tells you everything.

The fields existed because someone once asked "can we track X?" and the answer was always yes. Never "should we?" Never "will anyone query this?"

So you end up with fields like "Lead Source Detail" that has 47 unique values, 31 of which are variations of "website." "Buying Committee Role" that's empty on 89% of records. "Campaign First Touch" that nobody has filtered by since 2024.

I ran a query: which fields actually appear in our segments, reports, or automation triggers? Nine. Nine fields do all the work.

So I kept those nine, added two that were missing (last intent signal date and enrichment confidence score), and archived the rest.

The result wasn't just cleaner data. Reps started filling in the fields that matter because the form wasn't a wall of inputs anymore. Enrichment scripts run faster because they're writing to fewer columns.

Every field you add to a CRM is a tax on every person and every automation that touches that record. Audit yours. I bet half of them are dead weight.
posts.cta: How many fields on your main CRM object? And how many actually drive a decision?

inspired_by.author: Tara Robertson
inspired_by.summary: We finally killed our 47-field Salesforce opportunity object. Cut it to 11 fields, made them all required, and CRM hygiene went from 34% to 91% in 6 weeks. The lesson: your reps aren't lazy, your data model is punishing them. Clean architecture beats enforcement every time.

remixes.label: field-autopsy
remixes.hook: I ran a query on our CRM last Tuesday: which fields were updated in the last 90 days? The answer killed 14 of them.
remixes.body:
I ran a query on our CRM last Tuesday: which fields were updated in the last 90 days? The answer killed 14 of them.

Out of 23 contact fields, 14 hadn't been touched in three months. Not queried. Not filtered. Not referenced in a single report or automation.

They were ghosts. Taking up space in every import template, every CSV export, every new rep's onboarding confusion.

The worst offender: "Lead Source Detail" with 47 unique values. I pulled the list. 31 were variations of "website" spelled differently. Website. Web Site. web. Inbound - Website. WEB. You get the picture.

Here's how CRM bloat actually happens. Someone in a meeting says "can we track X?" and the answer is always yes. A new field gets created in 30 seconds. Nobody asks "will this field inform a decision?" Nobody asks "who will maintain data quality here?"

Creating a field is instant. Maintaining it is forever.

I deleted the 14 fields on a Wednesday. Nobody said a word until Friday, and only because I mentioned it in standup. Three days of silence is the ultimate audit.

Now I run the same query monthly. Any field untouched for 60 days gets flagged. Any field with more than 10 freetext variations gets a picklist or gets cut.

Clean CRM isn't a project. It's a practice.
remixes.cta: When's the last time you audited which CRM fields actually get used? Not which ones exist. Which ones matter.

remixes.label: data-debt-framing
remixes.hook: Technical debt has a cousin nobody talks about: data debt. And your CRM is where it compounds.
remixes.body:
Technical debt has a cousin nobody talks about: data debt. And your CRM is where it compounds.

Every field someone adds "just in case" is a liability. It clutters imports. It confuses new reps. It makes every integration mapping session twice as long. And worst of all, it gives the illusion of data richness while delivering data noise.

I inherited a CRM with 23 fields on the contact object. Sounded reasonable until I looked at utilization. Nine fields drove actual decisions: scoring, routing, segmentation, reporting. The other 14 were artifacts of past curiosity.

"Lead Source Detail" had 47 unique values because it was freetext. "Industry" was a picklist with options like "Other" used in 60% of records. "Competitor" was filled in for exactly 11 contacts.

Data debt works like technical debt. Each field is cheap to add. The cost is in maintenance, confusion, and the slow erosion of trust in your data. Reps stop filling things in because there are too many fields. Then ops stops trusting the data because it's incomplete. Then leadership stops using the reports because the data is unreliable.

The fix isn't a one-time cleanup. It's a rule: every new field needs a decision it informs and an owner who maintains it. No decision, no field.
remixes.cta: What's your worst CRM field? The one that exists but nobody can explain why.

posts.title: AI infra layer collapsing
posts.hook: Twelve months ago my enrichment pipeline needed five vendors. Today it needs two API keys and a Python script.
posts.body:
Twelve months ago my enrichment pipeline needed five vendors. Today it needs two API keys and a Python script.

The AI infrastructure layer is collapsing and the people selling picks and shovels are pretending it isn't.

I used to run: Clearbit for firmographics, Apollo for contacts, a waterfall tool for email verification, Clay for orchestration, and Zapier to glue it together. Five bills. Five dashboards. Five places where data could break.

Now I run a single Python script that calls two APIs directly, writes to SQLite, and a coding agent handles the edge cases. Total cost went from ~$2,800/mo to ~$340/mo.

This isn't because I'm some wizard. It's because the models got good enough to replace the middleware. The "integration layer" that these platforms sold was always just API calls with a UI on top. Once an agent can write and debug those API calls faster than you can configure a drag-and-drop workflow... the UI stops being worth the premium.

The platforms that survive will be the ones with proprietary data, not proprietary workflows. If your entire value prop is "we connect A to B," you're competing with a Claude Code session that costs $0.12.

Own the data or own the relationship. Everything in between is getting compressed.
posts.cta: Which tools in your stack are you quietly replacing with scripts?

Here's every SaaS tool I cancelled in the last 12 months and what replaced it. The pattern should worry vendors.

Clearbit for firmographics. Replaced by direct API calls to open data sources plus an LLM for parsing.

A waterfall email verification tool. Replaced by a Python script that hits two verification APIs in sequence. Cost dropped 80%.

Clay for orchestration. Replaced by a Python script with a config file. Same logic, no GUI, no seat-based pricing.

Zapier for glue work. Replaced by cron jobs and webhooks. Took an afternoon to set up. Runs for free.

Apollo stayed. It has proprietary contact data I can't replicate with scripts.

That's the dividing line. Tools with proprietary data survive. Tools that are workflow wrappers around APIs get eaten.

If your product is "we call an API and show you the results in a nice dashboard," your moat is a design choice, not a data asset. And design choices get replicated by a coding agent in an afternoon.

The infrastructure layer between raw APIs and end users used to be a viable business. That layer is compressing to near-zero for anyone with basic scripting ability.

The vendors who survive will be the ones who own data you can't get elsewhere. Everyone else is selling convenience on borrowed time.
remixes.cta: Which category does your favorite tool fall into: proprietary data or workflow wrapper?

remixes.hook: The 'picks and shovels' pitch for AI tools made sense 18 months ago. The shovels are dissolving.
remixes.body:
The 'picks and shovels' pitch for AI tools made sense 18 months ago. The shovels are dissolving.

Every investor deck in 2024 had the same thesis: don't bet on which AI model wins, bet on the infrastructure around it. The orchestration layer. The enrichment middleware. The integration platform.

Solid logic at the time. The problem: AI models got good enough to BE the infrastructure.

I used to need Clay to orchestrate a multi-step enrichment flow. Now I describe the flow in natural language and a coding agent writes the script. The orchestration layer was valuable because building it yourself was hard. Building it yourself isn't hard anymore.

I used to need Zapier because connecting two APIs required understanding webhooks, auth, and error handling. Now I say "when this webhook fires, call this API and store the result" and working code appears in minutes.

The pattern repeats everywhere. Any tool whose value was "we made a hard technical thing accessible via UI" is losing its moat as AI makes the hard technical thing directly accessible.

This doesn't kill all SaaS. Tools with proprietary data, network effects, or regulatory compliance still have real moats. But pure workflow-layer tools? Their TAM is shrinking every month.

If you're building in this space, the honest question is: can a motivated person with a coding agent replicate my core value prop in a weekend?

posts.title: Outbound measuring wrong things
posts.hook: Your outbound dashboard measures sends, opens, and replies. None of those are pipeline.
posts.body:
Your outbound dashboard measures sends, opens, and replies. None of those are pipeline.

I tracked my last 90 days of outbound. 4,200 emails sent. 38% open rate. 4.1% reply rate. Looks healthy on paper.

But when I mapped replies to actual pipeline created, 71% of replies were objections, OOO, or "not interested." The reply rate was a vanity metric disguising a 1.2% interested-reply rate.

So I rebuilt the tracking.

Now I measure three things:

✅ Interested reply rate (not total reply rate)
✅ Days from first touch to meeting booked
✅ Meeting-to-opportunity conversion by persona

The first metric killed two of my campaigns immediately. High reply rate, almost zero interested replies. The sequences were provocative enough to get responses but not relevant enough to get meetings.

The second metric showed that my best persona converts in 4 touches over 11 days. My sequences were running 7 touches over 21 days. I was over-nurturing by 10 days.

The third metric revealed that Directors convert to opportunity at 2x the rate of VPs. So I shifted volume toward Directors and let VPs get warmed through content instead.

Same send volume. Pipeline went up 40% in one month. The data was always there. The dashboard just wasn't showing it.
posts.cta: What's the one metric that actually changed how you run outbound?

inspired_by.summary: Most outbound teams are measuring the wrong thing. They optimize for sends and replies when they should be optimizing for pipeline-to-close rate by persona. Shared a framework we used to cut sequences by 60% and double qualified pipeline. The counterintuitive truth: less volume with tighter ICP beats spray and pray every time.

remixes.label: reply-taxonomy
remixes.hook: I categorized every outbound reply from the last 90 days. 71% of my 'replies' were people telling me to go away.
remixes.body:
I categorized every outbound reply from the last 90 days. 71% of my 'replies' were people telling me to go away.

Here's what a 4.1% reply rate actually looks like when you dissect it:

- 29% positive or curious replies. Actual conversations.

posts.title: Coding agents on real tasks
posts.hook: I stopped benchmarking coding agents on toy problems. Here's what matters when you use them on production work 8 hours a day.
posts.body:
I stopped benchmarking coding agents on toy problems. Here's what matters when you use them on production work 8 hours a day.

I've used Claude Code as my primary dev environment since March. Not as an autocomplete. As the thing that writes, tests, and ships the code while I direct.

The benchmarks comparing coding agents on algorithmic puzzles miss the point entirely. Production work is messy. It's "read these 14 files, understand the data flow, then add a column to this pipeline without breaking the three downstream consumers."

What actually differentiates these tools:

🔧 Context window management. Can it hold your whole system in memory or does it forget the schema by step 5?
🔧 Tool use discipline. Does it reach for the right file reader, or does it cat everything through bash like a freshman?
🔧 Plan-then-execute. Does it think before writing, or does it start coding immediately and refactor three times?
🔧 Recovery from errors. When a test fails, does it diagnose the root cause or just retry the same approach?

The agent that wins isn't the one that writes the cleverest function. It's the one that understands your codebase well enough to make a change that doesn't break anything else.

That's a fundamentally different skill than solving LeetCode.

remixes.body:
Coding agent benchmarks test if AI can solve puzzles. Production work tests if AI can survive your codebase.

These are completely different skills.

I've been shipping production code through Claude Code since March. Not toy projects. Real systems with messy state, legacy patterns, and undocumented dependencies.

What benchmarks measure: can the agent solve a self-contained algorithmic problem with clean inputs and a known correct answer?

What production requires: can the agent read 15 files across 4 directories, understand why a pattern exists (not just what it does), make a change that doesn't break three other things, and handle the fact that the test suite only covers 40% of the actual behavior?

The gap is enormous.

Where coding agents genuinely excel in production: orchestration tasks. "Read these five config files, generate a new module that follows the same patterns, write the tests, and update the imports." Tasks where the hard part is context management, not algorithmic creativity.

Where they still struggle: anything requiring understanding of WHY code is structured a certain way. Refactoring decisions. Architectural tradeoffs. The kind of judgment that comes from knowing the business context behind a technical choice.

The best mental model isn't "AI developer." It's "extremely fast junior developer who reads everything but understands nothing about your business." Direct accordingly.

remixes.body:
Six months of using a coding agent as my primary dev environment. Here's my honest scorecard.

Context: I run Claude Code 6-8 hours a day. It writes, tests, and ships code while I direct. Not autocomplete. Full agentic coding.

What works (genuinely faster than doing it myself):
- Boilerplate and scaffolding. Creating new modules that follow existing patterns. 10x faster.
- Multi-file edits with a clear spec. "Update this interface everywhere it's used." Would take me an hour, takes 3 minutes.
- Test writing. Especially when the implementation exists and you need coverage. Tedious work, perfectly suited for agents.
- Data transformation scripts. CSV parsing, API response mapping, format conversion. Boring work done fast.

What doesn't work (I take the keyboard back):
- Architectural decisions. The agent will confidently build the wrong abstraction if you let it.
- Debugging subtle state issues. It pattern-matches on symptoms instead of reasoning about causes.
- Anything requiring business context. It doesn't know why the code is shaped that way.
- Large refactors without a detailed plan. It drifts and makes inconsistent choices across files.

Net assessment: I ship roughly 3x more working code per day. But I spend more time reviewing and directing than I used to spend writing. The skill shifted from typing code to specifying intent precisely.

The people getting the most value aren't the best programmers. They're the best specifiers.

posts.title: Content strategy vs content blog
posts.hook: You have a blog. You do not have a content strategy.
posts.body:
You have a blog. You do not have a content strategy.

I know because I made the same mistake for a year. Published weekly. Hit keywords. Got traffic. Generated almost zero pipeline from it.

The blog was answering questions that strangers Googled. The content strategy should have been moving known prospects from "aware of the problem" to "ready to buy this specific solution."

Two completely different jobs.

So I rebuilt the system. Every piece of content now maps to one of three stages:

1. Problem recognition. "You're spending $92/lead on Google LSA and 33% are disqualified before you pick up the phone."
2. Solution education. "Here's how referral-based acquisition works and why it costs 2.7% CAC instead of 15%."
3. Decision acceleration. A case study, a calculator, a comparison. Something that shortens the last mile.

The blog still exists. But it feeds into email sequences, gets repurposed into LinkedIn posts, and gets sent directly to prospects who match the topic.

Content that just sits on your domain waiting for Google to send someone is not a strategy. It's a library with no librarian.

The system matters more than the individual post. Distribution matters more than production. And pipeline attribution matters more than page views.

I mapped out the exact 5-stage content motion we used to drive 38% of closed-won deals from content touches in Q2. Most teams are stuck at the top of the funnel because they never built the middle.

remixes.label: traffic-trap
remixes.hook: Your blog traffic graph looks great. Your pipeline chart tells a different story.
remixes.body:
Your blog traffic graph looks great. Your pipeline chart tells a different story.

I published 48 posts in 12 months. Organic traffic tripled. We ranked on the first page for a dozen keywords our ICP searches.

Total pipeline from those 48 posts: two qualified opportunities. Two.

The problem was targeting. Every post was optimized for strangers at the top of funnel. People who would never buy. Meanwhile, the 200 accounts already in our CRM never saw a single piece of content designed to move them from "considering" to "let's talk."

Content strategy isn't about publishing cadence or keyword volume. It's about mapping every piece to a specific stage of a specific buyer's journey. The blog post that ranks #1 on Google might generate zero revenue. The ungated teardown you email to 50 warm accounts might close three deals.

I stopped writing for Google and started writing for the 200 accounts that actually mattered. Traffic dropped 40%. Pipeline tripled in the next quarter.

The content didn't change that much. The targeting did. I went from broadcasting to the internet to narrowcasting to the accounts already in motion.
remixes.cta: What percentage of your content is actually aimed at accounts already in your pipeline?

remixes.label: reverse-funnel
remixes.hook: Most founders build their content funnel top-down. I accidentally proved it works better bottom-up.
remixes.body:
Most founders build their content funnel top-down. I accidentally proved it works better bottom-up.

For a year, I wrote awareness content. Broad topics, big keywords, educational angle. The theory: attract strangers, nurture them, convert them. Classic inbound.

Then I wrote one case study. A detailed breakdown of how we solved a specific problem for a specific type of company. I sent it to 30 prospects who were stalling in our pipeline.

Four of them booked calls that week.

That single bottom-of-funnel piece generated more pipeline than six months of blog posts combined. Not because the blog posts were bad. Because they were aimed at people who weren't ready to act.

So I flipped the model. Started with decision-stage content. Teardowns, ROI calculators, implementation guides. Things that help people who already know they have the problem decide whether we're the right solution. Then I worked backward toward awareness.

The counterintuitive result: the bottom-up approach actually generated better top-of-funnel content too. When you understand what closes deals, you write better hooks.

posts.title: Assistants to autonomous agents
posts.hook: The companies that deployed AI as "assistants" in 2024 are about to get lapped by the ones redeploying them as autonomous agents in 2026.
posts.body:
The companies that deployed AI as "assistants" in 2024 are about to get lapped by the ones redeploying them as autonomous agents in 2026.

I see this in my own stack. Last year, I used Claude to help me write emails. Draft something, I'd edit it, send it manually. Assistant mode.

Now my content pipeline runs like this: a cron job pulls transcripts, an agent extracts voice patterns, another agent drafts across four platforms, a dispatch system queues them for approval, and I just say "approve" or "edit." I'm the reviewer, not the operator.

The delta between those two setups isn't incremental. It's a different operating model.

But most companies are stuck in assistant mode because they skipped the hard part: defining the decision boundaries. What can the agent do without asking? What requires a human gate? What's the rollback if it gets it wrong?

Without those guardrails, autonomous agents are terrifying. With them, they're force multipliers.

The pattern I keep seeing: teams that invested in structured data, clean APIs, and clear process documentation in 2024 are the ones successfully deploying autonomous agents now. Everyone else is still fighting with prompt engineering on top of messy systems.

Clean pipes before smart water.
posts.cta: Where in your workflow have you moved from AI-assisted to AI-autonomous? What made the transition possible?

The failure modes are completely different. Assistant failures are embarrassing. Operator failures are lawsuits. The engineering rigor gap between the two is enormous and most teams aren't ready.

remixes.label: capability-ceiling
remixes.hook: Using AI to "help you write emails faster" is like buying a CNC machine to cut sandwiches.
remixes.body:
Using AI to "help you write emails faster" is like buying a CNC machine to cut sandwiches.

Most companies deployed AI in 2024 as a productivity boost for existing workflows. Draft this email. Summarize this document. Help me write this proposal. The human stayed in the loop for every step.

That was the right move then. Trust was low. Capabilities were unproven. You needed humans checking everything.

But 2026 is a different world. The companies pulling ahead aren't using AI to make humans 20% faster. They're building systems where AI runs entire workflows end to end, with humans stepping in only for judgment calls.

In my own stack, the difference is stark. Last year I used Claude to help draft content. Now a cron job triggers an agent that pulls transcripts, extracts patterns, generates drafts across four platforms, and queues them for review. I went from spending 3 hours on content to spending 15 minutes approving or editing what agents produced.

The humans didn't disappear. They moved upstream. From doing the work to designing the system and making the calls the system can't make.

The gap between "AI-assisted" and "AI-autonomous" isn't incremental. It's architectural. And the companies that don't make the leap will wonder why their competitors seem to have three times the team.
remixes.cta: What's one workflow in your org that's still in assistant mode but ready for autonomy?

remixes.label: trust-architecture
remixes.hook: The hardest part of moving from AI assistants to AI agents isn't the technology. It's trusting a system to act without asking you first.
remixes.body:
The hardest part of moving from AI assistants to AI agents isn't the technology. It's trusting a system to act without asking you first.

I've been running autonomous AI workflows for months now. Content pipeline, data enrichment, daily ops scans. They run on crons, produce outputs, and only surface to me when something needs a decision.

But getting here required building trust incrementally. I didn't go from "help me write this email" to "run my entire content operation" overnight.

posts.title: First 100 signups autopsy
posts.hook: I tracked every one of my first 87 signups to Clearbox. 52 of them came from a single Reddit thread.
posts.body:
I tracked every one of my first 87 signups to Clearbox. 52 of them came from a single Reddit thread.

Not an ad. Not a launch post. A genuine answer to someone asking how to monitor Reddit for sales opportunities. I described what I was building, linked to it, and moved on.

That thread converted at 11%. My landing page from LinkedIn? 2.3%. ProductHunt? 0.8%.

The lesson isn't "Reddit good, LinkedIn bad." The lesson is that conversion follows context. Someone actively asking about the exact problem you solve is 5x more likely to sign up than someone scrolling a feed.

So I built the entire GTM motion around that insight. Instead of broadcasting to everyone, I built a system that finds people in the moment they're describing the problem. Reddit, Hacker News, niche Slack communities, X threads.

The math is simple. 10 high-context conversations per day convert better than 1,000 impressions. And they cost almost nothing.

Of those 87 signups, 34 are still active after 60 days. The ones from Reddit retain at 2x the rate of the ones from paid channels. They came in with the right expectations because they found the product in context, not through a pitch.

Distribution channels aren't equal. The ones where people are already talking about the problem will always outperform the ones where you're interrupting.

posts.title: Intent signals vs Clay loops
posts.hook: Everyone's building Clay to Smartlead to Slack alert loops. Almost nobody is asking whether the intent signal is real.
posts.body:
Everyone's building Clay to Smartlead to Slack alert loops. Almost nobody is asking whether the intent signal is real.

I built one of these loops three months ago. Looked beautiful. Account shows intent on G2, Clay enriches the contact, Smartlead sends the sequence, Slack pings me when they reply.

Booking rate: 0.4%.

The problem wasn't the automation. The problem was the signal. G2 "intent" turned out to be someone's intern comparing 15 vendors for a report nobody would read. Bombora intent meant someone on the company's IP range visited a vaguely related blog post.

So I ripped out the third-party intent and replaced it with first-party signals.

Someone replies to a Reddit thread about solving the exact problem we solve. Someone's job posting mentions a tool in our integration stack. Someone publishes a blog post about the challenge our product addresses.

Those signals are harder to collect. You can't buy them from a data vendor. You have to build scrapers, write classifiers, and maintain the pipeline yourself.

But the booking rate went from 0.4% to 3.8%.

The automation layer is a commodity now. Anyone can build the Clay loop in an afternoon. The competitive advantage is in the signal quality feeding it. Garbage in, automated garbage out.

Your outbound automation is perfect. Your intent data is garbage. That's why you're booking 0.4%.

I know because I built the beautiful automation stack. Clay enrichment. Smartlead sequences. Slack alerts. Every handoff was clean. Every step was documented.

Booking rate: 0.4%.

So I stopped blaming the automation and started auditing the signal. What did "intent" actually mean in my pipeline?

G2 intent meant someone at the company visited a category page. Maybe an intern researching competitors for a slide deck. Maybe a bot. Maybe someone who already bought a competitor last month.

That's not intent. That's noise with a label.

When I replaced the third-party signal with first-party data, everything changed. Website visitors who hit the pricing page twice. Prospects who opened three emails and clicked a case study. People who actually engaged with my specific product, not a category.

First-party intent converted at 3.2%. Third-party G2 intent converted at 0.4%. An 8x difference from the same automation, same sequences, same copy.

The automation doesn't need fixing. The signal does. Before you optimize another email template, ask yourself: do I actually know this person wants what I'm selling, or did a data vendor tell me they might?

remixes.hook: I spent six weeks perfecting the plumbing. Then I realized the water was contaminated.
remixes.body:
I spent six weeks perfecting the plumbing. Then I realized the water was contaminated.

The plumbing: Clay to Smartlead to Slack. Beautiful enrichment flows. Perfect data handoffs. Automated sequences that triggered within minutes of a signal firing.

The water: G2 "intent" data. Which, after digging in, turned out to mean "someone at this company visited a page that might be related to your category at some point recently."

That's the signal I built an entire outbound motion around. No wonder the booking rate was 0.4%.

The GTM engineering community has a plumbing obsession. Every conference talk is about the stack. Clay this, Smartlead that, here's my 47-step enrichment waterfall. Nobody talks about signal quality because it's boring and hard to measure.

But signal quality is the only thing that matters. I've seen teams with ugly, half-manual processes booking 4% because they're reaching out to people who actually want to talk. And I've seen teams with gorgeous automation booking 0.3% because the signal is junk.

When I rebuilt around first-party signals, same automation, booking rate jumped to 3.2%. The plumbing didn't change. The water did.

Before you add another tool to your stack, audit the signal feeding it. If you can't explain exactly what the "intent" means in human terms, it's probably not intent.

posts.title: Niche down or die slow
posts.hook: I spent 8 months building a product for "anyone who does outbound." Then I talked to my 12 paying users and realized 9 of them were in the same vertical.
posts.body:
I spent 8 months building a product for "anyone who does outbound." Then I talked to my 12 paying users and realized 9 of them were in the same vertical.

The market was telling me something I didn't want to hear. I wanted to be a platform. The market wanted me to be a scalpel.

Niching down felt like shrinking. Like I was leaving money on the table. But the math said otherwise.

When I repositioned around that vertical, three things happened immediately:

1. The landing page conversion rate doubled because the copy spoke their language instead of generic SaaS talk.
2. Churn dropped because the product roadmap finally had a single customer to build for instead of trying to please everyone.
3. Word of mouth started working because people in the same vertical actually talk to each other.

The TAM got smaller on paper. Revenue grew faster in practice.

I think most early-stage founders resist niching because it feels like giving up optionality. But optionality without traction is just procrastination.

You can always expand later. You can't un-dilute a brand that stands for nothing.

The founder who owns one niche completely will always outperform the one who's "kinda relevant" to ten verticals. Depth beats breadth when you're small.

I spent 8 months building for "anyone who does outbound." Broad market, broad messaging, broad feature set. Classic platform approach. Then I talked to my 12 paying users and discovered 9 of them were in the same vertical.

The market was telling me something I didn't want to hear. I wanted to be a platform. The market wanted me to be a scalpel.

Here's my framework for when to niche down: if more than 60% of your paying users share a vertical, company size, or use case, you're already niched. You just haven't admitted it yet.

When I repositioned, the math changed immediately. Landing page conversion doubled. CAC dropped because messaging resonated with a specific person. Churn fell because the product actually fit the workflow. Word-of-mouth accelerated because people in a niche recommend solutions to each other.

My recommendation: don't niche down based on theory. Look at your data. Who pays, who stays, who refers. That cluster is your niche. Build for them first. You can always expand later from a position of strength. You cannot expand from a position of mediocre product-market fit across five segments.
tones.provocateur:
Every founder says they're "building a platform." What they mean is they're too scared to pick a lane.

I spent 8 months on this delusion. Built for "anyone who does outbound." The messaging was vague enough to apply to everyone and compelling enough to convert no one.

12 paying users. That's what 8 months of platform thinking got me.

Then I looked at who those 12 actually were. 9 were in the same vertical. Same size. Same use case. The market had been screaming the answer at me and I was too busy dreaming about TAM slides to listen.

Niching down felt like giving up. Like admitting the vision wasn't big enough. Every VC pitch deck says "$50B market." Nobody funds a deck that says "$200M niche where we'll own 15%."

But the second one is the real business. Because in a niche, you convert 3x better. You churn 50% less. Your customers do your marketing for you because they talk to each other.

The "platform" with vague positioning and 5% conversion? That's the company that runs out of money proving product-market fit across 6 segments simultaneously.

Pick the niche. Win the niche. Expand from dominance. This is the way. The other path is slow death by dilution.

The market was telling me something I didn't want to hear. I wanted to be a platform. The market wanted me to be a scalpel.

Niching down felt like shrinking. Like I was leaving money on the table. But the math said otherwise.

When I repositioned around that vertical, three things happened immediately:

1. The landing page conversion rate doubled because the copy spoke their language instead of generic SaaS talk.
2. Churn dropped because the product roadmap finally had a single customer to build for instead of trying to please everyone.
3. Word of mouth started working because people in the same vertical actually talk to each other.

The TAM got smaller on paper. Revenue grew faster in practice.

I think most early-stage founders resist niching because it feels like giving up optionality. But optionality without traction is just procrastination.

You can always expand later. You can't un-dilute a brand that stands for nothing.

The founder who owns one niche completely will always outperform the one who's "kinda relevant" to ten verticals. Depth beats breadth when you're small.
